title: Brooklyn jazz sites in the Linking Lost Jazz Shrines interviews
about: One entry per place on the Semantic Lab wikibase that is in the Linking Lost Jazz Shrines project and located in Brooklyn. Summaries, people and active dates were written by a model reading only the project's interview passages and wikibase statements for that place; they are a reading of the oral histories, not checked against outside sources. Every person and place carries its wikibase QID. address, latitude and longitude give the place's first location; locations lists them all where a place has more than one. Coordinates are decimal degrees (WGS84).
connectedness: How connected a place is inside the project's data, as a rough measure of importance. score runs 0 to 100 and rank 1 is the most connected. Half the score comes from linked_entities (distinct people, groups, organizations and places joined to it by a statement, in either direction), a quarter from interviews (how many different interviews mention it) and a quarter from mentions (how many transcript blocks tag it). Each part is on a log scale against the largest value among these places. linked_people counts the people and music groups among the linked entities; statements counts the linking statements. Only links inside the Lost Jazz Shrines project are counted.

sites.name: 78 Club
sites.address: 78 Herkimer Place, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: 78 Herkimer Place, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: Club 78 was a small upstairs club at 78 Herkimer Place, owned by a man the speakers know only as Scottie, who as far as Randy Weston recalls also brought in the talent. Weston describes an intimate room with a stage, reached by a flight of stairs, and a lot of good music; he went there to hear Cecil Payne while still working in the restaurant business, before he imagined becoming a musician, and says he played there himself. The story both of his tellings return to is the night Charlie Parker was due to play: Teddy Reig brought him in too intoxicated to perform, and a circle of neighborhood elders, including the sculptor Jimmy Gittens and Fred Braithwaite Sr., with Max Roach also furious, threatened to throw Reig down the stairs. Reggie Workman confirms the address, and Ed Stoute notes the building is now a church. The interviewers rank it among Brooklyn's top jazz rooms.

active.basis: Wikibase years 1947 to 1953, also on Weston's and Roach's statements; the passages answering the interviewer's question about its years are not in the dossier.

sites.name: Amsterdam News
sites.address: Marcus Garvey Boulevard & Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Marcus Garvey Boulevard & Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY
2340 Frederick Douglass Boulevard, New York, NY 10027

sites.summary: The Amsterdam News was a newspaper, and the interviews treat its Brooklyn side as part of the neighborhood's music life. Randy Weston says the Brooklyn Amsterdam News sat in the Holland Studio building at what is now Marcus Garvey Boulevard and Fulton Street, a building full of studios where kids came for lessons; his second piano teacher, Professor Atwell, worked there. He uses it to make a larger point: Brooklyn families had little money, yet nearly every home had a piano and every child studied some art. Weston names Tommy Watkins as the paper's editor. Willard Jenkins asks whether the clubs showed up in its nightlife columns and whether readers could learn who was playing from it, and Weston agrees they could. Harold Valle mentions something that came out of the paper in 1949.

active.basis: Wikibase start year 1909 and no end year; Valle cites the paper in 1949, and Weston recalls its Brooklyn office from his youth.

sites.name: Arlington Inn
sites.address: Fulton Street & Arlington Place, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Fulton Street & Arlington Place, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: The Arlington Inn was a bar with live music at the corner of Fulton Street and Arlington Place, one of a cluster of clubs on Fulton that people could walk between. Dickie Habersham-Bey counts it among five or six bars on one block, around the corner from the Baby Grand. Alma Carroll spent a great deal of time there as a young woman, at hours her mother would not have approved of, and remembers organist Wild Bill Davis playing where passers-by could see him through the window. Jo Ann Cheatham saw Thelonious Monk there in her late teens and says he earned his living in Brooklyn after losing his Manhattan cabaret card. Others rate it lower: Jimmy Morton says it had good local players but no big names, Ed Stoute calls it King Curtis's hangout, and Sam Pinn grades it a C. The site is now a laundromat.

sites.name: Art Theater
sites.address: 956-958 Marcy Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11216

locations.address: 956-958 Marcy Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11216

sites.summary: The Art Theater, which Randy Weston places on Marcy Avenue at Fulton Street, was one of the black theaters Weston lists alongside the Regent on Gates Avenue. Musicians played there, often at benefits, though Weston notes a theater left little stage space and the house kept only an upright piano. His sharpest memory is of a benefit he played after inviting his mother and father: a man named Arif, of a group called the Jolly Stompers, jumped up mid-show, bottles began flying at the stage, and Weston had to leap down from the piano and lead his parents out the exit. He says gangs met there and that fights at dances were routine, so players learned to look for the exits first. Jimmy Morton adds that the building is now a church.

active.basis: No years given; Weston tells it among memories of his early big-band and dance years, and Morton says it is now a church.

sites.name: Baby Grand Brooklyn
sites.address: 1274 Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY 11216

locations.address: 1274 Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY 11216

sites.summary: The Brooklyn Baby Grand stood on Fulton Street at Nostrand Avenue, on the same side as the Blue Coronet but further along, and Ed Stoute says it had the same owners as the Harlem Baby Grand and Town Hill. Stoute, hired around 1960 after leaving the Army, describes a front bar and a back room with three shows a night: a comic MC, a shake dancer, a rock or blues singer and a jazz singer, backed by his trio; having to learn each new show's tunes is where he says he really developed. Randy Weston and Lem Davis, the alto player who was also the musicians' barber, ran Sunday concerts there from 1954 as Jazz At Its Best, including a one-dollar show with Max Roach and Betty Carter. Alma Carroll remembers Big Maybelle, Joe Carroll and a brief go-go period, and Donald Sangster calls King Curtis a regular. Stoute says top groups drew limousines until the 1960s riot left it dead.

sites.name: Ben's
sites.address: Lexington Avenue & Sumner Avenue, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Lexington Avenue & Sumner Avenue, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: Ben's was a bar at Lexington and Sumner Avenue (now Marcus Garvey Boulevard) that Ed Stoute remembers from gigs with the baritone saxophonist Harold Cumberbatch, who hired him for jobs around this part of Brooklyn. Stoute calls it a joint, and what he recalls most is its battered upright piano, so far gone that many keys were missing. He mentions it in the same breath as Paul's on DeKalb, which he thought the nicer room. Willard Jenkins raised it in a group interview, and Stoute was the only one to answer; nobody else describes the music or the crowd.

active.basis: Neither the wikibase nor Stoute gives any year or period for Ben's.

sites.name: Berry Brothers (music venue)
sites.address: Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: The Berry Brothers was a club on Fulton Street, which Ed Stoute and Jimmy Morton place across from where Boys & Girls High School now stands. Alma Carroll ties it to the Berry Brothers act, calling it their club and saying it closed just before she arrived in Brooklyn. Stoute remembers it as a place that had music off and on, part of a Fulton and Nostrand scene that also took in the Tip Top, the Continental and the Moulin Rouge. Bob Myers recalls passing the Berry Brothers' couple of bars on his walk down Nostrand toward Fulton, and Jitu Weusi, speaking of the early 1960s, lists it among the neighborhood bars that only occasionally booked a player and were later ruined by the drug trade. Asked who played there, Reggie Workman answered only that some of everybody did. Speakers disagree on whether it had already closed.

sites.name: Bickford's Restaurant
sites.address: Fulton Street & Nostrand Avenue, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Fulton Street & Nostrand Avenue, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: Bickford's was a small luncheonette near the corner of Fulton Street and Nostrand Avenue, the kind of place Joe Long compared to Chock Full O' Nuts. It mattered as an after-hours meeting point: Bob Myers remembers that musicians went there once their gigs ended to talk about the music, and that as a youngster he wanted to be part of that talk. He ties the corner to the 1962 Freddie Hubbard record named for Fulton and Nostrand, though he is only fairly sure the luncheonette was Bickford's. Joe Long places it two doors from Birdel's record shop on Fulton Street. In the mid-1950s he and Wally Roker, bass singer of the Heartbeats, met there for coffee and tea, and Roker urged him to ask Birdel's for a job, which became Long's start in the music business. The two speakers place it slightly differently.

sites.name: Birdel's Records
sites.address: Fulton Street & Throop Avenue, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Fulton Street & Throop Avenue, Brooklyn, NY
Fulton Street & Nostrand Avenue, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: Birdel's was a record shop, and Joe Long tells its whole history in his interview. He first bought 78s at its location on Fulton Street and Throop, next to the Brooklyn Apollo. Later it moved to Fulton and Nostrand, where vocal groups making records would drop by. Wally Roker of the Heartbeats talked Long into asking owners Benjamin and Bertie Steiner for work. Long started part time around 1956-57. After riots and pressure from activists, the Steiners sold the store to Long in 1968. He grew it to three stores and later built an international vinyl trade, known for the saying that if Birdel's lacked a record, no one had it. Jazz musicians such as Miles Davis, Wilbur Ware and Randy Weston came in while playing the Blue Coronet. Later Biggie dug through old 45s in its basement. Long marked 50 years in 2007 before closing.

sites.name: Brooklyn Academy of Music
sites.address: 30 Lafayette Avenue

locations.address: 30 Lafayette Avenue

sites.summary: The Brooklyn Academy of Music (BAM), on Lafayette Avenue, is remembered in the interviews as a major performing-arts house rather than a club. Alma Carroll did consulting there for Mikki Shepard and, in return, got her husband Joe Carroll booked; she then handed Dizzy Gillespie a contract backstage at the Monterey Jazz Festival, and he headlined a BAM show called Steps in Time with the Copacetics and Peg Leg Bates. At a later BAM show Shepard had the Carrolls reseated so that Eubie Blake sat between them. Bob Myers presented his yearly New Cookers showcase at the BAM Café, with the Strickland brothers, Robert Glasper and Kenyatta Beasley. Ed Stoute treats a Sunday evening at BAM as a gig that calls for a suit, and Jo Ann Cheatham saw Maurice Brown there.

sites.address: 1531 Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY 11216

locations.address: 1531 Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY 11216

sites.summary: The Brooklyn Apollo was a theater on Fulton Street that mixed films with live acts. Randy Weston recalls cowboy pictures alongside Bessie Smith and Duke Ellington shorts and an amateur night, and saw it as a sign of a strong black community. Jitu Weusi describes its bills as a step below the Manhattan Apollo, with southern blues acts such as Bobby Bland especially popular, and remembers Mighty Sparrow there when he was a kid. Joe Long bought records at Birdel's, which stood next door around 1956-57. Speakers place it at Throop and Fulton; Jo Ann Cheatham corrects Tulivu-Donna Cumberbatch, who wondered whether a theater at Bedford and Arlington Place, where her father took her to afternoon jazz shows, had been the Apollo.

sites.name: Brooklyn Children's Museum
sites.address: Bedford Avenue & Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Bedford Avenue & Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: The Brooklyn Children's Museum enters the interviews through the building at Bedford Avenue and Eastern Parkway. Reggie Workman says the museum used a former auto showroom there as a temporary home while its own building was rebuilt, that musicians gradually became involved with it, and that once the museum moved out the vacated showroom became an African American cultural center, The Muse, keeping the museum's menagerie and a planetarium. He credits Bill Barron, Chris White and Rudy Collins with proposing its music program. Bob Myers describes it slightly differently, calling The Muse itself the museum's temporary home from 1968 to 1977, with jazz taught as part of children's workshops and Workman among the instructors.

active.basis: Wikibase start year 1899; Workman says the museum has been rebuilt and still exists; Myers dates the Muse arrangement 1968 to 1977.

sites.name: Brooklyn Conservatory of Music
sites.summary: The Brooklyn Conservatory of Music was a music school. Two people interviewed taught there. Bob Myers says Enos Payne had run its jazz department, and that after Payne left he needed a place to give piano and vocal lessons. That led Myers and Payne to start a Tuesday vocal jam session at Myers's club. Wade Barnes taught at the Conservatory in the early 1980s. He says he and faculty members first took a band into the schools from there, the start of the school program he later ran with Cecil Payne.

active.basis: Wikibase start year 1897 and no end year; Barnes taught there in the early 1980s.

sites.summary: The Brooklyn Palace was a dance hall on Atlantic Avenue that Randy Weston pairs with the Sonya Ballroom as one of the two places people went to dance. Donald Sangster says the big bands played there a lot, and he owns a flier, given to him by Leonard Gaskin, from when Andy Kirk played there in 1937-38. The speakers disagree on the corner: Sangster puts it at Atlantic and Bedford, while Ed Stoute says Atlantic and St. Marks. When the interviewer asks what happened there, the dossier gives no answer.

sites.name: Brooklyn Paramount Theater
sites.address: 385 Flatbush Avenue Extension, Brooklyn, NY 11201

locations.address: 385 Flatbush Avenue Extension, Brooklyn, NY 11201

sites.summary: The Brooklyn Paramount was a downtown theater, now part of Long Island University, that presented jazz concerts and revues alongside the dances and big bands Randy Weston recalls. Harold Valle saw Dinah Washington there in a blond wig and remembers her joke about crossing an open manhole on Flatbush Avenue; he locates the theater on DeKalb Avenue, while the wikibase gives the Flatbush Avenue Extension. Donald Sangster first heard Charlie Parker there, on a bill with Stan Kenton's band. For these listeners it was where big-name touring acts could be seen in Brooklyn.

active.basis: Neither the wikibase nor the speakers give years for the concerts described.

sites.summary: Brownies was a neighborhood bar with music in Crown Heights or Bed-Stuy, remembered mostly as a name in lists of the many clubs within walking distance. Speakers cannot agree on where it stood: Ed Stoute puts it on St. Marks Avenue between Nostrand and New York Avenues, Jo Ann Cheatham says Nostrand in one interview and a little side corner of Bergen Street in another, adding that a bar may still be there. Kwesi Mensah Wali counts it among the clubs of his teenage neighborhood, and Sam Pinn names it among the places where his interest in jazz grew. Cheatham went there in the mid-1990s with the drummer and dancer Scoby Stroman, as part of her own entrance into the jazz scene. Tulivu-Donna Cumberbatch had only heard of it. No one describes the room or who played there.

active.basis: No wikibase years; Cheatham went there with Stroman in the mid-1990s, and Mensah Wali and Pinn place it in their youth without years.

sites.summary: The Carroll Bar was a small joint on Fulton Street between Verona Place and Nostrand Avenue, a little before the Verona Cafe, where Ed Stoute went to hear tenor saxophonist Lucky Emmett and pianist James Sykes. He calls them heavy drinkers but formidable players. What made the room memorable was their trap for visiting horn players: they invited guests to sit in, called a tune like Cherokee, and took it very fast in an unexpected key, B-natural instead of B-flat in one telling, D in another, so the newcomer scuffled through the melody and then sat down. Stoute tells the story in two interviews, and his details on the key differ.

sites.summary: Club 243 was a jazz club and dance hall on Flatbush Avenue Extension, just before Myrtle Avenue, upstairs over a car dealership. Ed Stoute says Metrotech later bought out the whole property. In his memory it mixed Brooklyn musicians with players from everywhere. He uses it as an example that no Brooklyn venue was ever for local players only. Joe Knight, a small bass player named Eddie Hamilton and Stoute himself all played there. Tulivu-Donna Cumberbatch played there near the end of its run with the Baritone Saxophonists, a group started by John Stevenson and her father, Harold Cumberbatch. She remembers a huge floor that was good for dancing and a good stage. Harold Valle only names it in a list of clubs.

sites.summary: Club La Marchal was a small corner club at President Street and Nostrand Avenue. Harold Mabern says a hundred people packed it. It is remembered almost entirely for one event, the live recording known as The Night of the Cookers. Larry Ridley explains that the Club Jest Us, a group of musicians' wives that included Estelle Timmons, Brenda Hubbard and Cedar Walton's wife, rented the room to promote their husbands. Freddie Hubbard put the band together with Lee Morgan, James Spaulding, Mabern, Ridley and Big Black, and Orville O'Brien taped two crowded nights; Rudy Van Gelder later remastered the tapes. Otherwise speakers call it a weekend spot or a supper club with no steady jazz policy; Ed Stoute brought bands in and rated it B-list. Jitu Weusi thought it had come and gone by the early 1960s, though Spaulding dates the recording to 1965. The building is now apartments.

sites.summary: Concord Baptist Church, on what is now Gardner C. Taylor Boulevard, comes up in the interviews as one of the Black churches that opened its doors to jazz. Bob Myers names it among the congregations in the ecumenical wing of the Central Brooklyn Jazz Consortium, and says the committee approached it first because the music was held in esteem there: its pastor, Rev. Gardner Taylor, saw the Black church as the keeper of the culture and jazz and gospel as branches of one tree. Tulivu-Donna Cumberbatch lists it with St. Phillips, the House of the Lord and Siloam as churches that have hosted jazz presentations. Jimmy Morton adds an older tie: he knew Max Roach from the time Roach played in the band at Concord, early in his Brooklyn start. The interviews describe its role rather than any particular concert.

sites.address: Kingston Avenue between Lincoln Place and St. John's Place, Brooklyn, NY

locations.address: Kingston Avenue between Lincoln Place and St. John's Place, Brooklyn, NY

sites.summary: The Flamingo Lounge, also called the Flamingo Club, was a bar on Kingston Avenue between Lincoln Place and St. John's Place that Vanessa Rubin calls an organ joint where everybody played. Jitu Weusi puts its high point around 1963 to 1965, with crowds every Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Michael Howard remembers it as an after-hours room where musicians came after other gigs and jammed until 2 or 3 in the morning, especially when Levi ran it and served food; he says the owners drove a Cadillac and were well known. Both Ed Stoute and Jo Ann Cheatham complain about the men's room, which could be smelled from the bar, yet Cheatham says it had the best musicians and that it lasted for ages. Keisha St. Joan sang there often, with Harold Vick, her cousin Percy France and a young Eric Reed. Stoute ranked it B-list.

sites.summary: The Blue Coronet, on Fulton Street across from the Slave Theater, is remembered as the top Brooklyn jazz club. sites.summary: The Continental was a strictly-jazz club on Nostrand Avenue between Prospect and Park Places, which several speakers call the place to be before the Blue Coronet. Donald Sangster, who arrived in 1954, calls it the hippest spot he ever saw, with the stage over the bar and Willie Jones usually on drums. He names Lee Morgan, a teenage Ray Draper, Cannonball Adderley, J.J. Johnson, Jutta Hipp, Sonny Stitt and Wynton Kelly as visitors, and says Miles Davis's $1,500 fee pushed admission to $1.25. Sangster says a man named Scottie owned it. Kwesi Mensah Wali lived behind it; in summer the back door stood open and he listened from his fire escape. Jimmy Morton caught Elmo Hope's piano stool as it slid off the stage. Reggie Workman worked there with Gigi Gryce, and Dickie Habersham-Bey's interest in jazz began with seeing Miles Davis there.

sites.summary: The East was a cultural and educational center for people of African descent at 10 Claver Place, founded in 1969 by Jitu Weusi, Al Vann and fellow teachers after the Ocean Hill-Brownsville strike and Weusi's ban from Pratt. Besides a bookstore, the Uhuru Sasa School, a food co-op and lectures, it presented radical jazz: Leon Thomas opened it, and Pharoah Sanders, Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Gary Bartz, McCoy Tyner and Sun Ra followed, with Sanders and Mtume recording there. Admission was for black people only; Elvin Jones walked out over it in 1973. No alcohol was served, Lottie Brown's kitchen fed hundreds, and Malcolm X and Coltrane murals hung on the walls. Speakers recall silent, then participatory audiences and a family feeling, and see Sista's Place, Jazz 966 and the New Muse's festival as heirs. Jimmy Morton was unsure whether it was more political or musical.

sites.summary: The Id was a large room at East New York Avenue and Utica Avenue, in a building that had been Satellite Caterers and is now a church. Jimmy Morton recalls going downstairs to reach it. sites.summary: The Jazz Spot was a small, recent club on Marcus Garvey Boulevard between DeKalb Avenue and Kosciusko Street, run by Lillithe Meyers and her daughter Tiecha Merritt. Speakers describe a cozy, clean, tasteful room with a brick wall and pictures, a counter for food and drink but no alcohol, and a backyard garden for outdoor jazz. Admission was affordable but higher than most. It ran themed series such as one featuring women players, and Danny Mixon, Kim Clarke, Joanne Brackeen, Lil Phillips and Bob Cunningham played there; Harold Valle hosted the Monday jam sessions and MC'd. Jitu Weusi says Meyers was inspired by the Central Brooklyn Jazz Consortium, but the spot sat beside the Eleanor Roosevelt housing projects, far from the subway, in a neighborhood unused to jazz, and never won local economic support. Tulivu-Donna Cumberbatch calls it short-lived; Michael Howard guesses five years.

sites.summary: Tony's Grand Dean, at Grand Avenue and Dean Street, was a plain local bar with a small kitchen and a back room where the music happened. Jimmy Morton says it was owned by an Italian family, the Bordellos, and that the dancer Vincent Jones talked them into making it a jazz spot and brought in the acts; Jones, Freddy Braithwaite Sr. and the artist Jimmy Gittins ran it. Admission was a dollar, and Morton, a law student who never paid, was told to announce the bands, which made him an MC; his early color slides document the scene. Monk played there often while barred from Manhattan clubs, unadvertised; the Modern Jazz Quartet, Mingus and Etta Jones came through. Morton and Randy Weston both recall a gang brawl: bottles flew, Monk kept playing, Gittins felled three men with one swing. Morton says it disbanded once Dorothy Kilgallen's column made it known.

sites.summary: Trios Restaurant, on Sumner Avenue (now Marcus Garvey Boulevard) between Putnam and Jefferson, grew out of Randy Weston's father's businesses. Frank Weston had a barbershop on the next block in the 1940s, where Randy shined shoes beside Cecil Payne's father's tailor shop, then a candy store with a window grill selling hot dogs, pickled pigs' feet and soursop, which he expanded into a restaurant with a counter and tables. Its draw was the jukebox: Randy stocked Monk, Sarah Vaughan and Billie Holiday next to Stravinsky, Bartok and Berg, an idea he got from George Russell. The project's tag inside the passages names it with Nostrand rather than Gates Avenue.

active.basis: No wikibase years; Weusi lists it among clubs still going around 1960-62.

sites.summary: Up Over Jazz Café was Bob Myers's club, opened in 1995 in an upstairs space of about 1,100 square feet in his brother Phil's building on Flatbush Avenue, above the Wing Wagon, which supplied the food; hence the name. Inspired by Bradley's in the Village, Myers billed it as Brooklyn's nothing-but-jazz club: a quiet listening room with a good acoustic piano, a cover at the door, phones off and talk kept down. It ran six nights a week: a Monday jam led by Eddie Allen and then Vincent Herring that drew students from The New School and William Paterson, Enos Payne's vocal session on Tuesdays, Hip Hop meets Jazz on Wednesdays with Robert Glasper, Bilal and Common, and Glasper's trio on Thursdays for about three years. Cedar Walton and Ronnie Mathews dropped in from nearby. James Spaulding recorded there twice, and Jo Ann Cheatham remembers its warm colors and good music.

sites.summary: The Valhal Jazz Pub, also called the ValHal Club, was a bar with music in Fort Greene, which Keisha St. Joan puts at Fulton Street and Lafayette Avenue and Vanessa Rubin at the little circle, across from Frank's; both say it is now Scopello's, an Italian restaurant. Harold Valle says the street was lined with bars serving Navy Yard workers during the Second World War, and the Valhal was the last to hold out. Rubin calls it one of her first places, where she worked a lot in a duo with Kim Clarke and Franklin Gordon; St. Joan, Torrie McCartney, Cumberbatch and Melvin Sparks also performed there. Jitu Weusi and Michael Howard remember it packed for hours with organ trios, Ed Green among them, though Weusi places it at Vanderbilt and Gates, which conflicts with the others.

sites.summary: The Verona Café, which Ed Stoute calls a little bar, stood on Fulton Street across from Verona Place; Willard Jenkins notes it is also written Café Verona in Amsterdam News clippings. Randy Weston, who places it in the late 1940s and early 1950s, heard Don Byas there with trumpeter Leonard Hawkins, whose big, fat sound he remembers, and also the alto player Pete Brown, a Brooklyn resident who taught many younger players, and pianist Marlowe Morris. Stoute recalls walking past, hearing a piano he never knew the place had, and finding Gil Coggins at it.

sites.summary: The Weeksville Heritage Center is the historical institution that sponsored this oral history project: interviewers tell speakers the recordings will go into an archive in its new building, and in 2008 Maxine Gordon, its jazz consultant, started the project by driving Randy Weston around Brooklyn. Jennifer Scott says the project is meant to bring out jazz history the site did not yet show. Bob Myers lists it as a partner venue of the Central Brooklyn Jazz Consortium. Speakers also argue with it: Alma Carroll asks what it says about early music and about the children of Weeksville, and Donald Sangster credits Pam Green's restoration but disputes calling it the first Black township. Richard Habersham-Bey says his anti-poverty program gave it money.

active.basis: Wikibase start 1838; Sangster places Weeksville in the 1840s, and speakers in 2008-2011 describe it as active and building.

sites.summary: The Willoughby Temple, also called the Universal Temple, is a Masonic temple at Willoughby and Nostrand Avenues that Ed Stoute says is still standing. Jimmy Morton thinks he saw Jackie McLean there and connects it with Franklin Skeete, an old Brooklyn bass player he grew up with.
